pieds-noirs.name: Pieds-Noirs
pieds-noirs.summary: An ethno-cultural group of French and other European descent born in Algeria under French colonial rule from 1830 to 1962, most of whom left for France during or after the Algerian War of Independence.

t-touan.name: Tétouan
t-touan.summary: City in northern Morocco near the Strait of Gibraltar with over 2,000 years of history, rebuilt in the late 15th century by refugees fleeing the fall of Granada.

pastilla.name: Pastilla
pastilla.summary: A Maghrebi meat or seafood pie made with thin warqa dough, a specialty of Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia later spread abroad by emigrants.

anglo-moroccan-treaty-of-1856.name: Anglo-Moroccan Treaty of 1856
anglo-moroccan-treaty-of-1856.summary: An 1856 treaty in which Morocco, pressed by British consul John Hay Drummond Hay, gave Britain major trade privileges, ended a state trade monopoly, and set customs tariffs at 10%.

essaouira.name: Essaouira
essaouira.summary: A port city on Morocco's Atlantic coast, founded in 1760 by Sultan Mohammed bin Abdallah as a planned hub for foreign merchants; called Mogador until the 1960s, it later became a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

james-richardson-explorer.name: James Richardson
james-richardson-explorer.summary: British explorer (1809–1851) known for expeditions into the Sahel region of the Sahara, who died near Kukawa, Bornu.

carthage-national-museum.name: Carthage National Museum
carthage-national-museum.summary: A national museum atop Byrsa Hill in Carthage, Tunisia, founded in 1875 to house finds from Alfred Louis Delattre's excavations of the ancient Punic and Roman city.

white-fathers.name: White Fathers
white-fathers.summary: A Catholic missionary society founded in 1868 by Charles Lavigerie, Archbishop of Algiers, focused on evangelization and education, primarily in Africa.

charles-lavigerie.name: Charles Lavigerie
charles-lavigerie.summary: French Catholic cardinal and missionary (1825–1892) who served as Archbishop of Carthage, founded the White Fathers missionary order, and campaigned against the African slave trade.

acropolium-of-carthage.name: Acropolium
acropolium-of-carthage.summary: Former cathedral atop Carthage's Byrsa Hill, built over ruins of a Punic temple; renamed Acropolium in 1993 and now used for concerts and events.

alfred-louis-delattre.name: Alfred Louis Delattre
alfred-louis-delattre.summary: French archaeologist and missionary, 1850 to 1932, who made major discoveries at the ruins of ancient Carthage, including an ancient necropolis, and founded its archaeological museum.

tripolitania.name: Tripolitania
tripolitania.summary: A historic region of Libya settled since antiquity, ruled in turn by Carthage, Rome, the Vandals, the Byzantines, and Muslim and Ottoman conquerors by the 15th century.

kabylia.name: Kabylia
kabylia.summary: Mountainous coastal region in northern Algeria and homeland of the Kabyle people, part of the Tell Atlas mountain range.

tiznit.name: Tiznit
tiznit.summary: A town on Morocco's Souss-Massa coast, founded in 1881 by Sultan Hassan I, and now the capital of Tiznit Province.

moknine.name: Moknine
moknine.summary: A town in Tunisia's Monastir Governorate, historically known for producing enamelled Berber jewellery.

djerba.name: Djerba
djerba.summary: Tunisian island in the Gulf of Gabès, the largest island in North Africa, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.

cloisonn.name: Cloisonné
cloisonn.summary: Ancient technique of decorating metalwork by using thin metal strips to separate compartments filled with colored enamel or inlaid gems, often used for jewelry and religious images.

husainid-dynasty.name: Husainid Dynasty
husainid-dynasty.summary: A Tunisian ruling dynasty of Greek origin from Crete, founded in 1705 by al-Husayn I ibn Ali under Ottoman suzerainty; it ruled Tunisia until the republic's founding in 1957.

list-of-beys-of-tunis.name: Bey of Tunis
list-of-beys-of-tunis.summary: Title of the rulers of Tunis from 1613, when the Muradid dynasty took power, until 1957, when the Husainid monarchy was abolished.

byrsa.name: Byrsa
byrsa.summary: The walled citadel and hill overlooking the Phoenician harbour of ancient Carthage, Tunisia.

louis-ix-of-france.name: Louis IX of France
louis-ix-of-france.summary: King of France from 1226 to 1270, also known as Saint Louis and the sole French king canonised as a Catholic saint. He led the Seventh and Eighth Crusades and was captured and ransomed during the Seventh.

eighth-crusade.name: Eighth Crusade
eighth-crusade.summary: A 1270 crusade led by Louis IX of France against the Hafsid dynasty in Tunisia; Louis died of dysentery shortly after arriving, and little fighting took place.

dar-batha.name: Dar Batha
dar-batha.summary: A former royal palace in Fez, Morocco, commissioned by Sultan Hassan I in the late 19th century and converted into a museum of historical arts and crafts in 1915.

riad-architecture.name: Riad
riad-architecture.summary: A garden courtyard divided into four quadrants around a central fountain, historically part of house and palace architecture in the Maghreb and al-Andalus, likely derived from Persian gardens.

battle-of-isly.name: Battle of Isly
battle-of-isly.summary: An 1844 battle in which French forces under Marshal Bugeaud routed a much larger Moroccan force near the Isly River, part of France's push to complete its conquest of Algeria.

thomas-robert-bugeaud.name: Thomas Robert Bugeaud
thomas-robert-bugeaud.summary: A Marshal of France and Governor-General of Algeria during its colonization, he won military successes but used extreme violence that caused outrage at the time.

abd-al-rahman-of-morocco.name: Abd al-Rahman of Morocco
abd-al-rahman-of-morocco.summary: Sultan of Morocco from 1822 to 1859 of the 'Alawi dynasty, who preserved Moroccan independence during a period of European colonization while supporting Algerian resistance against France.

beni-snassen.name: Beni Snassen
beni-snassen.summary: A Zenata Berber tribe with Arab factions living in northeastern Morocco, near the border with Algeria.

thomas-jefferson.name: Thomas Jefferson
thomas-jefferson.summary: Founding Father and third U.S. president (1801–1809) who wrote the Declaration of Independence and shaped Jeffersonian democracy, while enslaving over 600 people.

emir-abdelkader.name: Emir Abdelkader
emir-abdelkader.summary: An Algerian Islamic scholar and military leader who resisted French colonization from 1831 to 1847, later known for humane treatment of prisoners and for halting a massacre of Christians in Damascus in 1860.

french-conquest-of-algeria.name: French conquest of Algeria
french-conquest-of-algeria.summary: France's 1830–1847 campaign to seize and hold Algeria, beginning with a naval blockade and invasion of Algiers and ending with the defeat of resistance leader Abdelkader.

invasion-of-algiers-1830.name: Invasion of Algiers (1830)
invasion-of-algiers-1830.summary: A 1830 French military campaign that conquered the Regency of Algiers, ending its centuries-old rule and beginning the colonial period of French Algeria.

mascara-algeria.name: Mascara
mascara-algeria.summary: A city in Algeria founded in the 10th century, famous as the hometown of Emir Abd al-Qadir, leader of Algerian resistance to early French colonial rule.

treaty-of-tafna.name: Treaty of Tafna
treaty-of-tafna.summary: 1837 treaty between Emir Abdelkader and French General Bugeaud in which Abdelkader recognized French sovereignty while France recognized his authority over much of Algeria.

george-iv.name: George IV
george-iv.summary: King of the United Kingdom and Hanover from 1820 to 1830, known for his extravagant lifestyle and lavish patronage of Regency-era building projects.

omar-agha.name: Omar Agha
omar-agha.summary: Dey of the Regency of Algiers from April 1815 to September 1817, taking power after his predecessor's assassination.

stephen-decatur.name: Stephen Decatur
stephen-decatur.summary: A United States Navy officer (1779–1820) who became the youngest captain in Navy history and served in both Barbary Wars, the Quasi-War with France, and the War of 1812.

battle-off-cape-gata.name: Battle off Cape Gata
battle-off-cape-gata.summary: The first battle of the Second Barbary War, fought on 17 June 1815 off Spain's coast, in which Stephen Decatur's American squadron captured the Algerian flagship Meshuda.

ra-s-hamidou.name: Raïs Hamidou
ra-s-hamidou.summary: Algerian admiral and state-sanctioned corsair (c.1770 to 1815) credited with capturing up to 200 ships, among the last powerful Algerian figures before the French invasion.

battle-of-the-smala.name: Battle of the Smala
battle-of-the-smala.summary: An 1843 raid in which French cavalry under the Duke of Aumale captured Algerian resistance leader Abd el-Kader's personal camp, seizing thousands of followers and his possessions.

bombardment-of-mogador.name: Bombardment of Mogador
bombardment-of-mogador.summary: An 1844 attack by French naval forces on the Moroccan city of Mogador, now Essaouira, during the Franco-Moroccan War.

tlemcen.name: Tlemcen
tlemcen.summary: The second-largest city in northwestern Algeria, a historic center of the Maghreb blending Arab, Berber, Andalusi, and Ottoman influences.

nahda.name: Nahda
nahda.summary: A 19th- and early 20th-century cultural 'awakening' that flourished in Arab regions of the Ottoman Empire, especially Egypt, Syria and Lebanon.

kabyle-people.name: Kabyle people
kabyle-people.summary: Berber ethnic group indigenous to Kabylia in northern Algeria, the largest Berber population in Algeria, with a large diaspora especially in France.

berber-latin-alphabets.name: Berber Latin alphabet
berber-latin-alphabets.summary: An adaptation of the Latin script used to write the Berber languages, first created in the 19th century.

gustave-flaubert.name: Gustave Flaubert
gustave-flaubert.summary: French novelist (1821–1880) regarded as the leading figure of literary realism, best known for his 1857 novel Madame Bovary.

salammb.name: Salammbô
salammb.summary: An 1862 historical novel by Gustave Flaubert set in Carthage just before and during the Mercenary War, which became an English-language bestseller and revived interest in Carthage's history.

christian-tuxen-falbe.name: Christian Tuxen Falbe
christian-tuxen-falbe.summary: A Danish naval officer, archaeologist, explorer, cartographer and diplomat (1791–1849).

tagdemt.name: Tagdemt
tagdemt.summary: A town in Tiaret Province in north-western Algeria.

zawiya-institution.name: Zawiya
zawiya-institution.summary: An institution in the Islamic world associated with Sufi orders, serving as a place of worship, school, monastery or mausoleum, often linked to a founder or local saint's tomb.

christopher-silver-music-historian.name: Christopher Silver
christopher-silver-music-historian.summary: American academic, curator and writer based in Canada, known for research on the 20th-century cultural history of Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, especially Jewish-Muslim relations through music.

nineveh.name: Nineveh
nineveh.summary: Ancient city on the Tigris near modern Mosul, Iraq, and capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire; briefly the largest city in the world until it was sacked in 612 BC.

ernest-aim-feydeau.name: Ernest-Aimé Feydeau
ernest-aim-feydeau.summary: French writer (1821–1873), father of the comic playwright Georges Feydeau.

alawi-dynasty.name: Alawi dynasty
alawi-dynasty.summary: Morocco's ruling royal family since the 17th century, claiming descent from the Prophet Muhammad, who ruled as sultans until the 1912 French protectorate and became kings after independence in 1956.

treaty-of-fes.name: Treaty of Fes
treaty-of-fes.summary: Signed under duress by Sultan Abd al-Hafid in March 1912, it established the French protectorate over Morocco and sparked violent backlash known as the Intifada of Fes.

john-hay-drummond-hay.name: John Hay Drummond Hay
john-hay-drummond-hay.summary: British envoy to the Court of Morocco in the 19th century.

abdelaziz-of-morocco.name: Abdelaziz of Morocco
abdelaziz-of-morocco.summary: Sultan of Morocco from 1894 to 1908, of the 'Alawi dynasty, who tried to strengthen the government with new taxes and heavy French loans, provoking revolt and his 1908 deposition by his brother.

abd-al-hafid-of-morocco.name: Abdelhafid
abd-al-hafid-of-morocco.summary: Sultan of Morocco from 1908 to 1912 of the Alaouite dynasty, who deposed his brother Abdelaziz but became increasingly backed by France, eventually signing the protectorate treaty.

italo-turkish-war.name: Italo-Turkish War
italo-turkish-war.summary: An 1911–1912 war between the Kingdom of Italy and the Ottoman Empire, after which Italy took Libya and the Dodecanese islands; seen as a precursor to World War I.

dodecanese.name: Dodecanese
dodecanese.summary: A group of Greek islands in the southeastern Aegean Sea off the coast of Anatolia, with Rhodes as the dominant island since antiquity.

list-of-spanish-colonial-wars-in-morocco.name: Hispano-Moroccan War
list-of-spanish-colonial-wars-in-morocco.summary: One of several Spain–Morocco conflicts since 1492; this list records two wars by that name, one in 1790–1791 and another in 1859–1860.
list-of-spanish-colonial-wars-in-morocco.source_title: List of Spanish colonial wars in Morocco

hafidiya.name: Hafidiya
hafidiya.summary: A 1907-1908 coup in Morocco in which Abd al-Hafid seized power from his brother Abd al-Aziz, starting in Marrakesh and gaining Amazigh and religious scholars' support.

waqf.name: Waqf
waqf.summary: An inalienable charitable endowment under Islamic law, typically land or property donated for religious purposes and managed by a trustee, with its full legal form dating to the 9th century CE.

madani-el-glaoui.name: Madani El Glaoui
madani-el-glaoui.summary: Moroccan statesman (1860-1918) who built the power of the Glaoui family, serving four sultans and rising to Grand Vizier in 1908 before being dismissed in 1911 under French pressure.

thami-el-glaoui.name: Thami El Glaoui
thami-el-glaoui.summary: Pasha of Marrakesh from 1912 to 1956 and chieftain of the Glaoua Berber tribe, who allied with the French protectorate in overthrowing Sultan Mohammed V before later accepting his restoration.

andrew-belton.name: Andrew Belton
andrew-belton.summary: A British Army officer (1882–1970) who served in campaigns in South Africa and Morocco and was an early advocate of using aircraft for military purposes.

kabyle-myth.name: Kabyle myth
kabyle-myth.summary: Set of beliefs propagated by French writers during colonial Algeria claiming a fundamental distinction between Arab and Kabyle peoples, later used to justify colonial repression.

sanusiyya.name: Sanusiyya
sanusiyya.summary: A Sufi religious order founded in Mecca in 1837, influential across Libya and the eastern Sahara, that resisted colonial powers and whose founder's grandson became King Idris I of Libya.

mokrani-revolt.name: Mokrani Revolt
mokrani-revolt.summary: The largest local uprising against French rule in Algeria since the 1830 conquest, breaking out in 1871 when more than 250 tribes rose under Cheikh Mokrani and allies.

shikla.name: Shikla
shikla.summary: A garment Jews in Tunisia and elsewhere in the Maghreb were forced to wear, mainly between the 9th and 19th centuries, to set them apart from Muslims.

muhammad-ii-ibn-al-husayn.name: Muhammad II ibn al-Husayn (Mohammed Bey)
muhammad-ii-ibn-al-husayn.summary: The eleventh Husainid Bey of Tunis, ruling from 1855 until his death in 1859.

chechia.name: Chechia
chechia.summary: A traditional Tunisian headgear, a vermillion-red cap-shaped bonnet similar to a beret, historically worn wrapped in a turban until the 19th century.

dhimmi.name: Dhimmi
dhimmi.summary: A historical status for non-Muslims under Islamic rule, granting legal protections in exchange for a poll tax and loyalty to the state, alongside specific restrictions.

sign-of-tanit.name: Sign of Tanit
sign-of-tanit.summary: An anthropomorphic symbol of the goddess Tanit found across Carthaginian sites in the western Mediterranean, first documented on 19th-century excavated stelae at Carthage.

tanit.name: Tanit
tanit.summary: Chief goddess of ancient Carthage and consort of Baal Hammon, worshipped as goddess of wisdom, civilization and crafts, and defender of towns and homes.

baal-hammon.name: Baal Hammon
baal-hammon.summary: The chief weather god of ancient Carthage and Numidia, depicted as a bearded, ram-horned figure and worshipped across North Africa and the western Mediterranean; his cult partner was Tanit.
